title: Make fractions, decimals and algebra agree
source: Make fractions, decimals and algebra agree

chunks.text: Here is a worked teaching example for Make fractions, decimals and algebra agree. Solve the equality shown by the bars Three identical trays each hold one pouch and 2 loose counters. Every pouch contains the same number of counters. The three trays contain 21 counters altogether. How many counters are in each pouch? The top bar separates the total into three equal trays. The lower bar separates one tray’s seven counters into a pouch and two loose counters. Work through the example 1.

Let x be the non-negative whole number of counters in one pouch. Each tray holds x+2 counters, so 3(x+2)=21. 2. The three equal tray totals share the 21 counters equally. Divide both sides by 3: x+2=7. 3. Remove the 2 loose counters from each tray total: x=7-2=5. 4. Check the original story: each tray has 5+2=7 counters, and three trays have 3 times 7=21. The answer is a permitted whole-number count. Answer. Each pouch contains 5 counters.

title: Build a recurrence from a reversible step
source: Build patterns from reasons, not guesses

chunks.text: This section is called Build a recurrence from a reversible step. A recurrence expresses a new value using earlier values. For a route-counting problem, group routes by their last move. Remove that move and identify the smaller problem left behind. The groups must be disjoint, and every legal route must belong to one. Conversely, each allowed shorter route must extend in the stated way. This reversible connection is the proof behind the recurrence.

SEE IT The final tile gives two complete cases F(n) counts tilings of an n-cell strip using 1-cell and 2-cell tiles. Each tiling ends in exactly one of these two ways; removing or restoring the final tile gives a reversible match. The starting values are F(0) = 1 for the empty strip and F(1) = 1. Starting values are part of the rule. There is one empty sequence of moves, even though it contains no moves. That single starting object allows a first move to be appended once.

Counts at unreachable negative positions are zero. These conventions are not tricks: they describe actual possible and impossible histories. A040 and A081 are useful for seeing how a changed set of permitted moves changes the recurrence. Do not import a familiar sequence because the first few entries look similar. Different rules can agree for several early cases and then separate. Calculate small cases from the definition, explain the transition, and only then build a table. Check a later table entry by a different classification if possible.

An agreement between two independently justified methods is more informative than extending one guessed pattern twice. Before moving on, open your notebook. title: Remember enough information, but no more
source: Build patterns from reasons, not guesses

chunks.text: This section is called Remember enough information, but no more. A location alone may not determine the legal next move. If a rule depends on the previous move, the state must remember that move as well. If a route may not revisit a place, it may need to remember which places have already been visited. Combining histories that allow different futures can create illegal routes or lose legal ones. SEE IT Mark the first complete repeated state The state is the current remainder.

Starting at 0, four steps return to 0, so the same four-state cycle repeats. Each arrow label gives the new total and the remainder it leaves on division by 5. Once the state is adequate, histories with that same state can share a count. Update each state from the states that can lead into it, and keep the conditions on each transition visible. A053 uses a restricted running difference; A123 and A143 use repeated numerical rules.

The information needed for these processes is different, even though each can be organised by states. For a deterministic process, repeating the full state forces the same future, because the next state is determined by the current one. Repeating just one visible feature may not. If the process continues indefinitely and only finitely many states are possible, some state must eventually repeat, giving an initial nonrepeating segment followed by a cycle. Mark those two parts separately when finding a distant term.

The target position must be measured from the actual cycle start. Before moving on, open your notebook. In one sentence, name the mathematical relationship this section is making visible. Then draw the smallest model, table or example that would help you recognise the same idea in a new problem.

title: Classify game positions by their legal moves
source: Build patterns from reasons, not guesses

chunks.text: This section is called Classify game positions by their legal moves. In a finite take-away game, call a position winning if the player about to move can force a win against every response. Call it losing if that player cannot. For the usual rule that taking the last object wins, the empty position is losing for the player who would move next: the previous move has already ended the game. A position is winning if at least one legal move leads to a losing position.

It is losing if every legal move leads to a winning position. These statements describe perfect play, not a prediction about what an inexperienced opponent might choose. Build the smallest positions first, because each larger position depends only on smaller ones. N3.26 is a place to turn this classification into a strategy. Before moving on, open your notebook. title: Build patterns from reasons, not guesses
source: Build patterns from reasons, not guesses

chunks.text: Here is a worked teaching example for Build patterns from reasons, not guesses. Explain an L-shaped addition A square array of dots grows from 3 rows of 3 to 4 rows of 4. How many dots are added? Explain a rule for growing any n-by-n square to the next square, where n is a positive whole number. The coral row owns the corner dot. The purple part contains only the remaining column, so the two additions do not overlap. Work through the example 1. Keep all 9 original dots.

Add a bottom row of 4 dots. 2. The new right-hand column still needs 3 dots above that row. Do not count the bottom-right corner twice. 3. The addition is 4 + 3 = 7, so the next square has 9 + 7 = 16 dots. 4. For an n-by-n square, the new row has n + 1 dots and the rest of the new column has n dots. The increase is 2n + 1. This construction explains why consecutive square numbers differ by successive odd numbers. Answer.

7 dots are added; in general the increase is 2n + 1. Now cover the worked steps and reconstruct the reasoning in your notebook. Do not copy only the answer. Write the observation that made each next step possible, then compare your explanation with the worked example.

title: Translate position into value
source: Make every digit obey both its jobs

chunks.text: This section is called Translate position into value. A two-digit number with tens digit a and units digit b is 10a+b. A three-digit number is 100a+10b+c. The leading digit must be nonzero, while later digits may be zero unless the question forbids it. Write these allowed ranges beside the expression. A letter representing a digit is not an unrestricted algebraic unknown. SEE IT A digit’s position supplies its multiplier Each long rod is ten units.

Swapping 4 and 2 preserves the digit sum 6, but changes 42 into 24: their difference is 18. Reversal can create useful cancellation because corresponding place values exchange. Repetition can create a different simplification: a palindrome fixes some positions to be equal. But similar-looking patterns must still be translated from their own definitions. A055, A071 and A088 require different relationships between the positions. Start with the full value expression, then simplify; do not replace it by a rule remembered from another digit puzzle.

In a cryptarithm, use carries as extra constraints. The units column restricts the next carry, which restricts the tens column, and so on. A carry is a small whole number determined by the size of the column total. An equation that fits the written last digit may still have the wrong carry. A129 is useful for checking each column and then verifying the completed multiplication as a whole. Before moving on, open your notebook. title: Use information that survives rearrangement
source: Make every digit obey both its jobs

chunks.text: This section is called Use information that survives rearrangement. Because ten leaves remainder one on division by nine, every power of ten does too. A number therefore has the same remainder modulo nine as the sum of its digits. The corresponding divisibility-by-three rule follows for the same reason. Rearranging digits preserves their sum, so it preserves these remainder tests even though it usually changes the value. SEE IT Each place contributes one remainder per digit unit The purple cell is the extra one in each place-value unit.

Removing multiples of 9 leaves the digit sum; that sum may still contain another group of 9. Other divisibility rules depend on position. Divisibility by four depends on the final two digits because the contribution from all earlier places is a multiple of one hundred, and hence a multiple of four. Evenness depends only on the units digit. Combining a digit-sum test with an ending restriction can be much more effective than either alone. A100 and A108 are places to keep both kinds of information active.

Bounds often turn a remainder condition into an exact sum. If the allowed digits constrain a total to a short interval, perhaps only one multiple of the required divisor lies there. State the bounds and explain why they hold. A digit-product condition can be handled through prime factors instead; a zero digit makes the product zero, so positivity of the product can rule it out immediately. title: Organise counts, inventories and next-number
source: Make every digit obey both its jobs

chunks.text: This section is called Organise counts, inventories and next-number. searches Decide whether you are counting numbers, positions or occurrences. For an occurrence count, examine each place separately and add the contributions. A number with repeated copies of a digit then correctly contributes more than once. A043, A089 and A140 develop different forms of place-by-place bookkeeping. When counting numbers containing a digit, a complement may instead avoid repeated counting. For a digit inventory, compare requirements with the stock of each symbol.

A surplus of one digit does not automatically repair a shortage of another. Treat interchangeable orientations together only when the question explicitly permits the same physical mark to serve both roles. A036 rewards this distinction between written values and available pieces. The permitted physical operation is part of the mathematics. For ordinary positive integers, first compare the number of digits. Among numerals of the same length, the first differing digit decides which number is larger.

To find the next larger valid number of a fixed length, preserve the longest prefix that can still be completed as a larger valid number, increase the next digit by the smallest amount that permits a valid completion, and use the smallest legal suffix. Extra restrictions can make a sorted suffix invalid. A120 and A145 require careful control of the permitted digits and their positions.

Watch out for these • A leading zero shortens a numeral; a code may permit it, but an ordinary fixed-length number does not. • Divisibility by three or nine survives permutation, while an ending-based divisibility test may change. • When counting printed digits, repeated occurrences count separately; when counting qualifying numbers, each number counts once. Carry this idea forward Keep place value, digit restrictions and counting conventions separate until they can be combined precisely. Each surviving candidate must satisfy all three kinds of condition. Ready to try it?

title: Make every digit obey both its jobs
source: Make every digit obey both its jobs

chunks.text: Here is a worked teaching example for Make every digit obey both its jobs. Follow both carries Add 58 and 67. Explain what each carry means, and why the answer has a hundreds digit. The purple arrow carries one ten from the ones column. The coral arrow carries one hundred from the tens column. Work through the example 1. In the ones column, 8 + 7 = 15 ones. Regroup 10 ones as 1 ten, leaving 5 ones. 2.

In the tens column, the original 5 tens and 6 tens join the carried ten: 5 + 6 + 1 = 12 tens. 3. Regroup 10 tens as 1 hundred, leaving 2 tens. The answer is 1 hundred, 2 tens and 5 ones. 4. Check the value directly: 50 + 60 + 8 + 7 = 110 + 15 = 125. Each regrouping kept the total unchanged. Answer. 58 + 67 = 125. Now cover the worked steps and reconstruct the reasoning in your notebook. Do not copy only the answer.

title: Build an angle chain from dependable facts
source: Use angle relationships and exact geometric facts

chunks.text: This section is called Build an angle chain from dependable facts. Angles around a point total a full turn of 360 degrees, and angles on a straight line total a half turn of 180 degrees. An acute angle is greater than 0 degrees and smaller than 90 degrees, a right angle equals 90 degrees, and an obtuse angle is larger than 90 degrees but smaller than 180 degrees. Vertically opposite angles are equal because each is the supplement of the same adjacent angle.

Parallel lines create equal corresponding and alternate angles when crossed by a transversal. Identify which line directions form each angle before using one of these relationships. SEE IT A triangle’s angle sum becomes visible The added line passes through the top vertex and is parallel to the base. Alternate angles transfer α and β to the top; together with γ they make 180 degrees. A triangle's interior angles total half a turn.

One way to see this is to draw through a vertex a line parallel to the opposite side: the other two triangle angles appear beside the vertex angle along that straight line. Equal sides in an isosceles triangle give equal opposite angles. These facts can be chained, but every step must refer to the correct triangle or pair of lines. For a convex polygon, diagonals from one vertex split it into triangles without overlap. Counting those triangles gives the interior-angle sum.

A regular polygon also has equal angles and equal sides, which supplies more information than the angle sum alone. Do not use regularity merely because a drawing looks balanced. A016 is a useful place to distinguish what follows from equal-sided components from what only appears visually symmetrical. Before moving on, open your notebook. title: Connect angles on a circle to the arcs they see
source: Use angle relationships and exact geometric facts

chunks.text: This section is called Connect angles on a circle to the arcs they see. An arc is a portion of a circle's circumference between two points. Its measure is the central angle swept out along that arc; for a major arc this is a reflex angle greater than 180 degrees. Equal spacing around a circle gives equal central angles, so the size of an arc can be found by counting equal gaps. Count the gaps along the relevant arc, not the number of points encountered including both ends.

SEE IT Use the arc that does not contain the viewing vertex Both angles use endpoints A and C. The coral arc is 120 degrees around the centre, so the inscribed angle at B is 60 degrees. The other arc contains B and is not the arc used here. For three distinct points A, B and C on a circle, angle ABC is half the measure of the arc AC that does not contain B. To prove this, let O be the centre and D the point diametrically opposite B.

For a point P equal to A or C, but different from D, write α = angle PBD. The equal radii OB and OP make triangle BOP isosceles, so angle BOP = 180 degrees - 2α. Since OB and OD point in opposite directions, the arc PD avoiding B has measure 180 degrees - angle BOP = 2α. If A and C lie on opposite sides of diameter BD, add the two angles at B and the two arcs through D.

If they lie on the same side, take the absolute difference of the two angles and of the two arcs. In either case, the arc AC avoiding B has twice the measure of angle ABC. If A or C equals D, its angle and arc contribution are zero, so the same calculation still applies. The choice of arc is essential. The same two endpoints determine two arcs, and only the one not containing the viewing vertex belongs to that angle.

For a triangle with all vertices on a circle, the three gaps between successive chosen vertices control its three angles. N4.30 connects this fact with a complete counting argument. A strict inequality must remain strict when translated from angle size to arc size. Before moving on, open your notebook. title: Use coordinates or extra lines to make a proof visible
source: Use angle relationships and exact geometric facts

chunks.text: This section is called Use coordinates or extra lines to make a proof visible. An auxiliary line is a line added to your working because it exposes a known relationship. It may produce a perpendicular height, an isosceles triangle or two triangles with a shared base. Explain why the line helps before calculating. Adding many unrelated lines can make a diagram harder to read without creating any usable information. Coordinates offer another exact representation. Choose axes that match existing horizontal or vertical structure, then describe points by their positions.

Differences of coordinates describe movement between points. Equal coordinate changes can establish parallel directions; fixed horizontal or vertical lines reveal perpendicular distances. The coordinates are a model of the stated geometry, so choosing them must not introduce an unproved midpoint, equality or right angle. For any points X, P and Y, the triangle inequality says XP + PY ≥ XY. Equality holds exactly when P lies on the straight segment from X to Y.

Three positive lengths form a nondegenerate triangle exactly when each is shorter than the sum of the other two; for lengths ordered a ≤ b ≤ c, it is enough to check a + b > c. A reflection preserves distances, and every point on its mirror line stays fixed. Reflecting one endpoint can therefore turn a shortest broken route through a line into a straight-segment problem. Lattice diagrams require an additional distinction: a segment may pass through grid points between its endpoints.

A059 is a place to examine that structure instead of counting only visible endpoint pairs. Whether using coordinates, angle chasing or a construction, finish by relating the derived quantity to the requested one. A proof should explain why changing the drawing while preserving the facts would leave the conclusion unchanged.

Watch out for these • Do not infer a midpoint, a right angle or equal lengths from appearance alone. • For a circle angle, use the arc opposite its vertex; the other arc gives a different relationship. • Angles strictly below a threshold must not be mixed with angles equal to that threshold when counting cases. Carry this idea forward Use a small chain of justified geometric facts. A diagram suggests where to look; angle relationships, stated equalities and exact coordinates establish what is true. Ready to try it?

A016, A059, N4.30, K011 Before moving on, open your notebook. In one sentence, name the mathematical relationship this section is making visible. Then draw the smallest model, table or example that would help you recognise the same idea in a new problem.

title: Use angle relationships and exact geometric facts
source: Use angle relationships and exact geometric facts

chunks.text: Here is a worked teaching example for Use angle relationships and exact geometric facts. The angle outside a triangle Triangle ABC has angle A = 48 degrees and angle B = 67 degrees. Extend BC beyond C to D. Find angle ACD and check it using the two other triangle angles. The teal 65 degrees is inside the triangle. The purple 115 degrees is outside, between CA and the extension CD. Work through the example 1.

The triangle’s interior angles sum to 180 degrees, so angle ACB = 180 degrees - 48 degrees - 67 degrees = 65 degrees. 2. CB and CD point in opposite directions along one straight line. Therefore angles ACB and ACD sum to 180 degrees. 3. Angle ACD = 180 degrees - 65 degrees = 115 degrees. 4. Substitution explains a second check: 180 degrees - (180 degrees - 48 degrees - 67 degrees) = 48 degrees + 67 degrees = 115 degrees. An exterior angle equals the sum of the two non-adjacent interior angles. Answer. Angle ACD = 115 degrees.

title: Use bases, heights and complementary regions
source: Measure the region or solid that matters

chunks.text: This section is called Use bases, heights and complementary regions. A triangle has area bh/2, where b is the chosen base and h is its perpendicular height. Two congruent copies can form a parallelogram with base b and height h, explaining the factor of one half. A sloping side is usually not the height. If a vertex moves along a line parallel to the base, the perpendicular height stays fixed, so the area stays fixed too.

SEE IT Area depends on perpendicular height The two triangles share the same base. Their top vertices lie on a parallel line 3 cm above it, so sliding the vertex changes the shape but leaves the area at 9 cm squared. Triangles with a common height have areas in the same ratio as their bases. Triangles with a common base have areas in the same ratio as their perpendicular heights. These comparisons can avoid finding either area separately.

An unknown height may also disappear when two distances add to a known total. A047 and A152 reward choosing useful bases and heights before attempting to measure sloping edges. When a shaded region is awkward, calculate its complement inside an easier whole. A018 is a place to organise the outside pieces and check that they neither overlap nor leave gaps. If regions do overlap, adding their areas counts the intersection more than once. Use the contribution reasoning from Chapter T06 to correct the total.

The same arithmetic can describe a union or an exactly-one region, but the required correction differs. Before moving on, open your notebook. title: Separate boundary change from scale change
source: Measure the region or solid that matters

chunks.text: This section is called Separate boundary change from scale change. Perimeter counts exposed boundary length. Removing a piece removes some old boundary and may create new boundary. Compare those changes directly. A corner cut can replace horizontal and vertical lengths by equal new lengths, while a cut in the middle of an edge can create extra boundary. The removed area alone does not determine the perimeter change. Scaling every length by a factor k scales area by k squared and volume by k cubed.

A rectangle's two dimensions each receive the length factor; a rectangular solid's three dimensions each receive it. These relationships explain why doubling a length factor does not merely double area or volume. They apply to similar shapes and solids, where every relevant linear dimension changes by the same factor. A volume formula must match the solid. A prism with constant cross-sectional area A and height h has volume Ah because equal-thickness slices have equal volume.

For a submerged object's effect on a water level, the tank's cross-section at that level matters. A rectangular base by itself does not guarantee vertical sides. Keep assumptions such as full submersion, constant cross-section and no overflow explicit when using a displacement model. Before moving on, open your notebook. title: Count hidden pieces through layers and boundaries
source: Measure the region or solid that matters

chunks.text: This section is called Count hidden pieces through layers and boundaries. A drawing of a solid shows only some of its pieces. Decide whether the solid is filled, hollow, layered or merely a framework. A060, A087 and A106 use different layer descriptions. Find the number of pieces in one exact layer or slice, then explain how those slices cover the entire solid once. Visible squares on the outside do not directly count interior cubes.

SEE IT Hidden cubes belong to a layer too A layer has 3  times  2 = 6 cubes. There are 2 layers, including the lower cubes hidden by the upper layer in the oblique view, so the solid contains 12 cubes. For painted-cube questions, classify a small cube by which boundary faces it touches. Corners, edge interiors, face interiors and the interior of the block have different numbers of exposed faces. If one large face is unpainted, the classification changes at that face.

Counting unpainted cubes first can be easier, but any shortcut must respect small dimensions where an assumed interior row does not exist. For tunnels or removed portions, identify intersections before adding volumes. A cube lying in several tunnels must be removed only once. With three overlapping sets, subtracting all pairwise intersections removes their common intersection too many times, so its contribution must be restored appropriately. A037 develops this bookkeeping.

For a net such as A127, first determine which drawn lengths correspond to the same solid dimension, then calculate volume from the recovered dimensions. Watch out for these • A triangle height is perpendicular to the chosen base; it is not simply a nearby sloping edge. • A perimeter is the boundary that remains exposed, not the sum of boundaries of separated component pieces. • Do not count only visible cubes when the stated solid is filled. Explain a layer or coordinate classification that includes the hidden ones.

title: Measure the region or solid that matters
source: Measure the region or solid that matters

chunks.text: Here is a worked teaching example for Measure the region or solid that matters. A cut changes the boundary Start with two rectangles, each 6 cm by 4 cm. Remove a 1 cm by 1 cm square from a corner of one rectangle, and a 1 cm by 1 cm square from the middle of an edge of the other. What are the two new perimeters? Dashed grey segments are removed boundary. Coral segments are new exposed boundary. The unlabelled notch sides are all 1 cm.

Work through the example 1. Each original perimeter is 2  times  (6 + 4) = 20 cm. 2. The corner cut removes two old 1 cm boundary segments and exposes two new 1 cm segments. Its change is -2 + 2 = 0 cm. 3. The edge notch removes one old 1 cm boundary segment and exposes three new 1 cm segments. Its change is -1 + 3 = 2 cm. 4. The new perimeters are therefore 20 cm and 22 cm.

Both remaining areas are 24 - 1 = 23 cm squared, which shows why removed area alone cannot determine a perimeter change. Answer. Corner cut: 20 cm. Edge notch: 22 cm.
